title: Rheinmetall Cuts Outlook, Boeing Lands Jet-Powered JDAM Contract, Space Force Hedges SpaceX Bet
subhead: Rheinmetall slashes its 2026 sales forecast after Germany cancels a frigate program, Boeing wins the first production deal for a jet-powered 300+ nmi precision bomb, and the Space Force diversifies satellite tracking away from SpaceX with three smaller contracts — while a Heritage report warns US interceptor stocks are below 10% of what a China conflict would require.

sections.heading: Rheinmetall Cuts 2026 Sales Outlook After German Frigate Program Scrapped
sections.body:
Rheinmetall has lowered its 2026 sales outlook after Germany cancelled a planned frigate program that was expected to contribute significantly to revenue, Defense News reported on August 6, citing Reuters. The downgrade marks a rare stumble for Europe's most valuable defense company, which has ridden a defense-spending boom since Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

The scrapped frigate program was part of Germany's naval modernization agenda, and its cancellation removes a major revenue line from Rheinmetall's near-term pipeline. The company did not specify the revised sales target in the initial reporting.

Rheinmetall's stock has been one of the best performers in European defense since 2022, fueled by surging demand for ammunition, armored vehicles, and air defense systems. The outlook cut is a reminder that even the sector's winners remain exposed to national political decisions — in this case, Berlin choosing to cancel a major naval procurement rather than delay or restructure it.
sections.whyItMatters: Rheinmetall's downgrade is a signal that the European defense boom is not evenly distributed. Naval procurement cancellations can wipe out revenue lines just as fast as land-war demand creates them. For a company whose valuation reflects expectations of uninterrupted growth, even a modest outlook revision moves markets — and raises questions about whether Germany's defense spending commitments will translate into actual contracts on the timeline industry expects.

sections.heading: Boeing Wins First Production Contract for Jet-Powered JDAM LR
sections.body:
Boeing secured the first production contract for the jet-powered JDAM Long Range (JDAM LR), valued at $75 million, Defense News reported on August 6. The weapon extends the standard JDAM bomb kit with a jet engine, pushing its range beyond 300 nautical miles — a dramatic increase from the conventional JDAM's approximately 15-mile glide range.

JDAM LR converts existing 2,000-lb warheads into long-range precision strike weapons at a fraction of the cost of cruise missiles. The jet-powered variant gives strike aircraft and bombers the ability to engage targets from standoff distances comparable to JASSM, but using cheaper, more plentiful bomb bodies.

The contract comes as the US military is acutely aware of its long-range precision munition shortage. With JASSM and ATACMS inventories depleted by the Iran war, a low-cost, long-range alternative that uses existing bomb stockpiles addresses both the cost and volume problems simultaneously.
sections.whyItMatters: JDAM LR is a practical answer to the munitions shortage: instead of building more expensive cruise missiles from scratch, it stretches existing bomb inventories to 300+ nmi ranges. At a fraction of JASSM's per-unit cost, it could be produced in much larger quantities. The $75M initial contract is small, but the production potential is enormous if the Pentagon prioritizes it — which the Iran-war munitions drain gives every reason to do.

sections.heading: Space Force Hedges SpaceX Satellite Tracking Bet With Three Smaller Contracts
sections.body:
The US Space Force has awarded three contracts to smaller companies to develop alternative satellite tracking capabilities, hedging its reliance on SpaceX for aircraft tracking and space domain awareness, Defense One reported on August 6. The move comes as the military grows increasingly dependent on SpaceX's Starlink-derived tracking data while concerns about single-vendor dependence intensify.

The contracts represent a deliberate diversification strategy: rather than relying exclusively on SpaceX's constellation for tracking aircraft and other targets from orbit, the Space Force wants competing sensor networks that can provide resilient, redundant coverage. The specific companies and contract values were not detailed in the initial reporting.

The effort reflects a broader Pentagon discomfort with SpaceX's dominant position in military space. While SpaceX provides unmatched launch capacity and satellite coverage, the company's ownership structure and Elon Musk's unilateral decision-making — including reported restrictions on Starlink use in operational contexts — have made the military wary of single-source dependence.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the Space Force formally acknowledging that SpaceX dependence is a vulnerability, not just a convenience. The three-contract hedge is small in dollar terms but significant as doctrine: it signals the Pentagon is building redundancy into its space-based tracking architecture. If successful, the model could extend to other SpaceX-dominated capabilities, from communications to launch.

sections.heading: Heritage Foundation: US Has Less Than 10% of Interceptors Needed for China Conflict
sections.body:
A new Heritage Foundation report warns that the United States currently holds less than 10 percent of the PAC-3 MSE, THAAD, SM-6, and SM-3 interceptors required to deter or prevail in a protracted high-intensity conflict with China, Defense One reported on August 5. The figure is a stark quantification of the interceptor shortfall that has escalated from concern to crisis since the Iran war began consuming US missile defense inventories.

The report estimates that during the first four days of Operation Epic Fury, US and allied forces expended approximately 1,738 theater surface-to-air munitions defending against 565 Iranian ballistic missiles and 57 cruise missiles. Those four days alone consumed what CSIS Missile Defense Project director Tom Karako described as 'a decade worth of production' in some weapon categories.

The Trump administration signed a deal with Lockheed Martin in January to triple annual PAC-3 production to 2,000 missiles, and the Pentagon announced a $3 billion framework with Lockheed and Northrop Grumman on August 4 to boost PAC-3 solid rocket motor production and quadruple THAAD output. But Karako noted those targets were set before the Iran war's consumption rates became clear. Northrop says its Allegany Ballistics Laboratory investment has doubled motor production since 2021, with a goal of tripling by 2027.

Trump publicly denied the weapons shortage on August 6, telling reporters that the US has 'far more munitions than anyone in the world' and claiming 'leakers' were being 'hunted down,' BBC reported.
sections.whyItMatters: The Heritage report puts a number on what Pentagon planners have been saying privately: less than 10% of needed interceptors for a China scenario. The Iran war's consumption of 1,738 munitions in four days reveals a rate of expenditure that production scaling cannot match in any relevant timeframe. Even tripling Patriot and quadrupling THAAD production won't close the gap for years — and that's assuming no further combat consumption.

sections.heading: Firestorm Labs 3D-Prints Drones Aboard USS Essex Without Shore Resupply
sections.body:
Firestorm Labs manufactured more than 1,000 parts and 12 of its proprietary 3D-printable Squall drones aboard the Wasp-class amphibious assault ship USS Essex during its transit to RIMPAC 2026 in Hawaii, without any shore resupply, Military Times reported on August 5. The drones were assembled in 12-foot seas and later flown as adversary aircraft during counter-drone exercises.

The demonstration used Firestorm's xCell containerized microfactory — a factory-in-a-box deployable aboard Navy vessels to produce unmanned aerial systems and spare parts on demand. Service members also printed mechanical test components and fabricated repair parts needed by the Essex's crew.

The demonstration directly supports the Navy's 'containerized capability campaign plan' announced by Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle in March, which envisions transportable containers housing drones, weapons, and other capabilities deployable worldwide. The Pentagon separately announced framework agreements in May with Anduril, CoAspire, Leidos, and Zone 5 for over 10,000 containerized missiles over three years beginning in 2027 under the Low-Cost Containerized Munitions program.
sections.whyItMatters: Printing drones at sea in 12-foot waves without shore resupply is more than a stunt — it validates the Navy's containerized-warfighting concept at a moment when the service is worried about sustaining forces in contested waters far from logistics hubs. If xCell-type microfactories can produce drones and repair parts on demand, the supply chain for unmanned systems shifts from 'ship it from home' to 'print it on station.' That changes the logistics calculus for a Pacific conflict.

sections.heading: CBO: Trump-Class Battleship Program Will Cost $275 Billion Total, $23.4 Billion for First Ship
sections.body:
The Congressional Budget Office estimates the Trump-class battleship program will cost $275 billion in total across the planned fleet, with the first ship alone costing $23.4 billion, Defense News reported on August 5. The figures make it one of the most expensive surface combatant programs in naval history.

The CBO's cost estimate reflects both the technical complexity of modernizing the battleship concept — large, heavily armed surface combatants with advanced weapons systems — and the industrial base challenges of building ships this expensive in small numbers. The $23.4 billion first-ship cost includes non-recurring engineering, tooling, and production line setup that won't need to be repeated for follow-on vessels.

The program represents a philosophical bet on large surface combatants at a time when many naval strategists argue that distributed fleets of smaller, cheaper vessels are more survivable in an era of anti-ship missiles and drone swarms. The cost-per-unit also raises questions about how many ships Congress will ultimately fund.
sections.whyItMatters: $23.4 billion for a single ship is a staggering number that will dominate the Navy's shipbuilding budget for years. At that price, fleet size becomes a political question, not a naval one — Congress may authorize fewer hulls than the Navy wants, creating a gap between strategic ambition and industrial reality. The CBO estimate also gives ammunition to critics who argue the Navy should be investing in unmanned distributed systems rather than large, vulnerable surface combatants.

sections.heading: Iran Warns Gulf States They Will Be Hit If US Does Not Desist
sections.body:
Iran has warned Gulf states that they will be targeted if the United States does not cease military operations, Defense News reported on August 6, citing Reuters. The warning escalates Tehran's rhetoric against regional states that host US military bases and air defense systems, and comes amid an intensification of the US-Iran conflict that has consumed significant American munitions and air defense assets.

The threat directly addresses the Gulf states — particularly Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, and Bahrain — that have allowed the US to operate from their territory during the conflict. It raises the stakes for these governments, which must balance their security partnerships with Washington against Iranian military retaliation on their own soil.

The warning also intersects with the interceptor shortage: Gulf states depend on US-provided Patriot and THAAD batteries for air defense, and those systems are themselves running low on interceptors due to the same war that Iran is threatening to escalate.
sections.whyItMatters: Iran's threat to Gulf states is both a military and political calculation. Militarily, it raises the possibility of a wider regional war that would further strain US interceptor stocks. Politically, it tests the resolve of Gulf governments that have bet on American protection — at a moment when that protection is demonstrably thinner than it was six months ago because of munitions depletion.

bottomLine: Rheinmetall's outlook cut is a reminder that the European defense boom has casualties — cancelled programs can hit even the sector's biggest winners. Boeing's JDAM LR contract offers the Pentagon a mass-producible, long-range alternative to depleted cruise missile stocks. The Space Force's SpaceX hedge and Firestorm's at-sea drone printing both represent the same impulse: reducing dependence on fragile, centralized supply chains, whether in satellite tracking or munitions manufacturing. And the Heritage report's 'less than 10%' interceptor figure for a China scenario crystallizes what everyone in the Pentagon already knew — the Iran war has consumed munitions at a rate that production scaling cannot match for years.
sources: Defense News, Defense One, Military Times, BBC, Heritage Foundation, CSIS, Congressional Budget Office, Reuters
